p.seg: The tradition says:
"Heaven gives birth to all things,
Earth nourishes them,
and the sage completes them."
When merits and virtues combine,
the ways and arts arise.
Hence it is said:
He spreads out the sun and moon,
arrays the stars and constellations,
orders the four seasons,
harmonizes yīn and yáng,
distributes the vital breath and governs natures,
arranges the five phases,
so that spring brings life and summer growth,
autumn harvest and winter storage,
yáng generates thunder and lightning,
yīn forms snow and frost,
nurturing all living beings,
some flourishing, some perishing,
moistening them with wind and rain,
basking them with sunlight,
warming them with seasonal energy,
sending down killing frost,
positioning them with the multitude of stars,
controlling them with the Dipper's balance,
enveloping them with the six directions,
netting them with the guiding principles,
changing them through calamities and anomalies,
informing them through auspicious signs,
moving them with life and death,
enlightening them with patterns and writings.
Thus what is in Heaven can be seen,
what is on Earth can be measured,
what is in things can be recorded,
what is in humans can be read.
Therefore Earth demarcates the Five Sacred Mountains,
delineates the Four Great Rivers,
regulates marshes and lakes,
channels water sources,
plants vegetation and nurtures species,
envelops and propagates countless roots,
exposes forms and nourishes essences,
to establish all living beings,
not violating Heaven's timing,
not depriving things' natures,
not concealing their true dispositions,
not hiding their deceptions.
Thus those who know Heaven look up to observe celestial patterns,
those who know Earth look down to examine terrestrial principles,
the walking and breathing creatures,
the flying and crawling kinds,
the water-dwelling and land-traveling,
the root-anchored and leaf-growing types,
all have their hearts calmed and natures settled,
for Heaven and Earth sustain each other,
and the vital breaths interact and respond to complete them.
Thereupon the ancient sages looked up to observe celestial patterns,
looked down to examine terrestrial principles,
charted the cosmos,
to establish the human way,
and the people began to awaken,
knowing the intimacy between father and son,
the duty between ruler and subject,
the way between husband and wife,
the order between elder and younger.
Thereupon the hundred offices were established,
and the kingly way arose.
The people ate meat and drank blood,
clothed themselves in hides and furs;
until Shénnóng,
considering roaming insects and running beasts
difficult to nourish the people,
sought edible things,
tasted the fruits of various herbs,
examined the sour and bitter flavors,
and taught the people to eat the five grains.
The people under Heaven,
dwelling in wilderness and caves,
without houses,
lived in the same domains as birds and beasts.
Thereupon Huángdì felled trees and assembled timber,
built palaces and dwellings,
with beams above and eaves below,
to shelter from wind and rain.
The people knew dwelling in houses and eating grains,
but did not yet know productive labor.
Thereupon Hòujì demarcated territories,
drew boundaries,
to distinguish what the land was suitable for;
opened up land and cultivated grains,
to nourish the people;
planted mulberries and hemps,
produced silks and linens,
to cover their bodies.
At that time,
the four great rivers were not yet connected,
and floods caused harm;
Yǔ then channeled the rivers and dredged the waterways,
connecting the four great rivers,
leading them to the sea,
large and small drawing each other,
high and low receiving one another,
all streams flowing smoothly,
each returning to its place,
after which the people could leave the high dangers,
and dwell on level ground.
With valleys and streams crisscrossing,
and customs not yet communicated,
the nine provinces were cut off,
without the use of boats and carts,
to cross depths and reach distances;
thereupon Xī Zhòng bent wood to make wheels,
used straight pieces for shafts,
harnessed horses and yoked oxen,
floated boats and plied oars,
to replace human labor.
They smelted metal, carved wood, split reeds, and fired clay to prepare tools and vessels,
whereupon the people understood light and heavy,
favored benefits and disliked difficulties,
avoided toil and sought ease;
thereupon Gāo Yáo established prisons and set punishments,
hung rewards and instituted penalties,
distinguished right from wrong,
clarified likes and dislikes,
checked treachery and evil,
and eliminated excess and disorder.
The people learned to fear the law,
but lacked ritual and righteousness;
thereupon the middle sages established education in the Pìyōng and Xiángxù schools,
to rectify the rituals of high and low,
illuminate the rites between father and son, the duties between ruler and subject,
so that the strong would not bully the weak, the many would not oppress the few,
abandoning greedy and base hearts,
and promoting pure and clean conduct.
When ritual and righteousness were not practiced,
and guiding principles not established,
later generations declined and fell into ruin;
thereupon the later sages established the Five Classics,
clarified the Six Arts,
inheriting Heaven and unifying Earth,
exhausting affairs and examining subtleties,
probing emotions and establishing foundations,
to continue human relationships,
honoring Heaven and Earth,
compiling and cultivating writings,
handing them down to future ages,
extending them to birds and beasts,
to rectify decline and chaos,
combining the strategies of Heaven and humanity,
fully comprehending the fundamental way,
the wise penetrating its heart,
the hundred craftsmen exhausting their skills,
then harmonizing with the sounds of pipes, strings, silks, and bamboos,
setting up the music of bells, drums, songs, and dances,
to regulate extravagance,
rectify customs,
and communicate refinement and elegance.
Later generations became excessive and depraved,
adding the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
the people abandoned the root and rushed to the branch,
crafts and技巧 emerged recklessly,
intentions varied widely,
then adding carved patterns and engraved decorations,
applying glue, lacquer, cinnabar, blue-green, mysterious yellow, and marvelous jade colors,
to exhaust the pleasures of ears and eyes,
and extreme the skill of craftsmen.
Now donkeys, mules, camels,
rhinoceroses, elephants, hawksbill turtles,
amber, coral,
kingfisher feathers, pearls, jades,
born in mountains and hidden in waters,
choose their places to dwell,
pure, clear, bright,
moist, glossy, and smooth,
ground but not worn thin,
dyed but not blackened,
born by the celestial breath,
governed by divine spirits,
secluded, tranquil, pure, quiet,
floating and sinking with the spirits,
all serve with effort and are used,
exhausting their essence to become vessels.
Therefore it is said,
the sage completes them.
This is how they can unify things and comprehend changes,
govern emotions and natures,
and manifest humaneness and righteousness.
The superior person is broad and expansive in virtue,
vast yet meticulous,
attracting distant lands and pacifying those nearby,
embracing all states under heaven.
Thus, the sage embraces benevolence and upholds righteousness,
distinguishing the finest details,
contemplating heaven and earth,
remaining steadfast in peril,
and orderly in ease—
all through the governance of benevolence and righteousness.
Practicing it among kin brings joy to those afar;
cultivating it within the household spreads renown beyond.
Hence, no act of benevolence remains hidden or obscure—
none fails to shine forth.
Yú Shùn served his parents with devotion,
illuminating heaven and earth;
Bóyí and Shūqí starved at Shǒuyáng,
yet their virtuous deeds endure for millennia;
Lǚ Shàng rose from commoner to the highest office,
his lineage enjoying noble rank for generations;
while Zhì Bó relied on force and authority,
annexing the three Jìn states only to perish.
Therefore, the noble person grasps the Way to govern,
relies on virtue to act,
sits upon benevolence,
and stands strong with righteousness,
embracing emptiness and tranquility,
moving through limitless transformations.
Thus, handling affairs with awareness of shortcomings leads to lasting benefit;
using the compass to draw circles,
the square to shape angles.
Sages rule the age,
the worthy establish merits:
Tāng elevated Yī Yǐn,
Zhōu employed Lǚ Wàng,
their actions harmonized with heaven and earth,
their virtue matched yīn and yáng,
executing heaven’s punishment against evil,
crushing violence and dispelling calamity,
nurturing life with vital energy,
radiating brilliant light,
hearing to the farthest reaches,
seeing in all directions,
promoting loyalty while rejecting slander,
establishing uprightness and eradicating corruption,
advancing the Way and halting wickedness,
preventing dualities from arising,
upholding fundamental order,
stamping out萌芽 before they sprout.
Those who plan affairs without benevolence and righteousness will ultimately fail;
those who build heights without securing foundations will collapse.
Thus, sages prevent chaos through classical arts,
as craftsmen straighten curves with plumb lines.
Virtue abundant brings widespread awe;
force abundant breeds arrogance.
Duke Huán of Qí achieved hegemony through virtue,
while the Second Emperor of Qín perished by relying on punishment.
Thus, cruelty accumulates resentment,
while virtue spreads and merits flourish:
the common people adhere through virtue,
kin bond through benevolence,
couples unite through righteousness,
friends trust through righteousness,
ruler and minister order themselves through righteousness,
officials serve through righteousness.
Zēngshēn and Mǐnzǐ achieved great filial piety through benevolence;
Bó Jī established ultimate chastity through righteousness;
rulers safeguard states with benevolence’s firmness;
ministers support rulers with righteousness’s steadfastness;
the ruler governs with benevolence,
the minister serves with righteousness;
communities thrive with benevolent sincerity,
courts function with righteous decorum;
beauties exemplify conduct through chastity,
martyrs illuminate names through righteousness;
yáng energy generates through benevolence,
yīn rhythm descends through righteousness;
"The Deer Cry" seeks its herd through benevolence,
"The Ospreys" call to mates through righteousness;
the Spring and Autumn Annals critiques through benevolence and righteousness,
the Book of Songs preserves or rejects through them;
the Qián and Kūn hexagrams harmonize through benevolence,
the Eight Trigrams succeed through righteousness;
the Book of Documents orders clans with benevolence,
ruler and minister define loyalty with righteousness;
the Rites fulfill duty through benevolence,
Music ascends and descends through ritual.
Benevolence is the guiding principle of the Way,
righteousness the learning of sages.
Those who learn it gain clarity,
those who lose it become obscured,
those who betray it perish.
Exert strength in position,
build merits through righteousness;
in military campaigns and formations,
virtue and benevolence provide stability,
righteousness brings strength;
harmonizing energy and nurturing nature,
the benevolent enjoy longevity;
ranking talent and virtue,
the righteous act with principle.
Noble persons praise each other with righteousness,
petty people deceive for profit;
fools create chaos by force,
the worthy govern through righteousness.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn states:
"Benevolence governs kinship,
righteousness benefits respect.
For ten thousand generations without disorder—
this is the governance of benevolence and righteousness."
Those skilled in discussing antiquity align it with the present;
those able to assess distant matters examine the near.
Thus, narrators recount the achievements of the Five Emperors
and reflect on themselves;
list the failures of Jié and Zhòu
and take personal warning—
then virtue may match sun and moon,
actions accord with spirits,
reaching heights and distances,
penetrating the obscure and hidden,
hearing the soundless,
seeing the formless,
where ordinary eyes detect no omens
nor comprehend the essence,
studying the roots and ends of the Five Classics,
the truth and falsehood of the Way and virtue,
grasping their meaning
yet not seeing their masters.
Conventional minds value what’s passed down from antiquity
and disdain present creations,
indifferent to what they see,
credulous of what they hear,
deceived by appearances,
missing inner truth.
Sages do not prize scarcity,
yet people despise abundance;
the five grains nourish life
but are discarded on the ground,
while useless pearls and jades
are treasured on their persons.
Sages value themselves over jewels—
thus Shùn cast gold into jagged mountains,
discarded pearls into lake depths,
to block lustful desires
and extinguish extravagant cravings.
The Way need not stem from remote antiquity
if its essence brings achievement.
The Spring and Autumn Annals excludes the Five Emperors above
and the Three Kings below,
recording minor virtues of Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn,
the twelve rulers of Lǔ—
yet its lessons suffice for modern governance
to understand success and failure;
why must we seek the Three Kings?
Thus, the ancients’ conduct
resembles our own.
Achievers do not stray from the Way and virtue,
as tuners never miss the notes;
heaven’s Way harmonizes the seasons,
humanity’s Way orders the five constants.
Duke of Zhōu shared auspicious signs with Yáo and Shùn,
the Second Emperor shared calamity with Jié and Zhòu.
King Wén was born among the Eastern tribes,
Great Yǔ emerged from the Western Qiāng—
eras and lands apart,
yet laws and measures aligned.
Thus sages and worthies unite with the Way,
fools join with disaster;
the virtuous receive blessings,
the wicked meet misfortune;
low virtue brings perilous position,
abandoning the Way spells ruin.
For ten thousand ages, the law unchanged—
past and present share one moral order.
Thus, fine horses are not limited to Qíjì,
sharp swords are not only Gānjiàng,
beautiful women are not solely Xī Shī,
loyal ministers are not just Lǚ Wàng.
Now, having a horse but lacking Wáng Liáng's driving skill,
having a sword but lacking the work of whetting,
having a woman but lacking adornments of fragrance and gloss,
having a scholar but not encountering a King Wén,
the Way and its methods accumulate but are not expressed,
beautiful jade is stored in a box and deeply hidden.
Therefore, those who embrace the Way need the right era,
those holding simplicity await the craftsman,
the Way is established for the wise,
horses are good for the skilled driver,
the worthy are employed by the sage,
eloquence is understood by the intelligent,
writings are transmitted by those who comprehend,
affairs are clear to those who see.
Hence, those who manage affairs follow their principles,
those taking medicine rely on its efficacy.
Writings need not originate from Confucius's school,
medicine need not come from Biǎn Què's prescriptions,
what fits is good,
can be taken as a model,
adapted to the times with flexible application.
So, when nature is hidden within a person,
their energy reaches the heavens,
from the minute to the vast,
learning below and understanding above,
things are grouped by kind,
sounds respond through tones,
the Way leads and virtue harmonizes,
benevolence establishes and righteousness arises,
the king practices it in court,
the commoner practices it in the fields,
to govern the branches, adjust the root,
to straighten a shadow, correct the form,
nourish the root and the branches flourish,
harmonize will and energy, and the Way flows.
Thus, those seeking the distant must not lose the near,
those managing shadows must not forget the substance,
when above is bright, below is clear,
the ruler sage, the ministers loyal.
Some aim far and lose the near,
some find the Way blocked and the path ended.
Jì Sūn coveted Zhuānyú's land,
and turmoil arose within his own walls.
Those advancing cannot ignore difficulties,
those planning affairs cannot fail in loyalty;
thus, when punishment is established, virtue scatters,
when flatterers are used, loyalty perishes.
The Book of Songs says:
"Correct your heart,
to nurture all states."
Meaning that with one heart, the world is transformed,
and the state is governed,
this is what it refers to.
Those in high positions must not be insecure in their stance,
those treading danger must not have an unsteady support.
Insecure stance leads to falling,
unsteady support leads to collapse.
Therefore, the sage, dwelling high above,
uses benevolence and righteousness as a nest,
facing peril and decline,
takes the worthy and sage as a staff,
thus high without falling,
in danger without collapse.
In ancient times,
Yáo used benevolence and righteousness as a nest,
Shùn took Yǔ, Jì, and Qì as his staff,
thus high and ever more secure,
active and ever more firm.
Resting in the security of height,
riding on the respect of humility,
virtue matching heaven and earth,
light covering the four corners,
achievements lasting endlessly,
name transmitted undying,
all because their stance found its nest,
their support found the right material.
Qín used punishments as a nest,
hence the disaster of a overturned nest and broken eggs,
took Zhào Gāo and Lǐ Sī as a staff,
hence the calamity of collapse and injury,
Why?
Those appointed were wrong.
Thus, leaning on sages leads to emperorship,
leaning on the worthy leads to kingship,
leaning on benevolence leads to hegemony,
leaning on righteousness leads to strength,
leaning on slander leads to ruin,
leaning on villains leads to demise.
Therefore, the rigid long endure but break,
the soft long endure and last,
the hasty and swift falter quickly,
the slow and steady remain constant,
the bold regret soon,
the gentle proceed with ease,
the impatient inevitably suffer loss,
the soft and meek overcome the hard and strong,
petty wisdom cannot handle great matters,
minor eloquence cannot persuade the masses,
merchants skillfully seek profit from trade,
yet bend integrity,
treacherous ministers delight in deceit,
flattering and covering faults,
but cannot act for public good,
hiding their cunning,
evading their duties.
Thus, the shortcomings of the wise
are not as good as the strengths of the foolish.
Duke Wén planting rice,
Zēngzǐ herding sheep.
Judging talent without thoroughness,
believing falsehoods and losing direction.
The overly perceptive miss some things,
the broad-minded contain all.
The simple and straightforward are near to loyalty,
the slick and clever are near to ruin.
The nobleman avoids dazzling colors,
rejects clamorous sounds,
abstains from rich flavors,
distances himself from fawning affections.
The Way of Heaven uses the great to control the small,
the heavy to topple the light.
Using the small to govern the great,
disrupts order and violates integrity.
Slanderers resemble the worthy,
sweet words seem trustworthy,
listeners are confused,
observers are blinded.
Thus Sū Qín was honored by the feudal lords,
Shāng Yāng was eminent in Western Qín.
Without a wise and intelligent ruler in the world,
who can discern their true form?
Therefore Yáo exiled Huāndōu,
Confucius executed Shàozhèng Mǎo;
sweet words are praised,
none are not swayed by them,
only Yáo knew their reality,
Confucius saw their truth.
Thus, those opposing sage kings are executed,
those obstructing worthy rulers are punished,
those meeting ordinary kings are honored,
those encountering chaotic times are glorified.
Zhèng Dān fled Qí and returned to Lǔ,
Qí had the fame of nine assemblies,
while Lǔ suffered the shame of Gānshí.
To hold a state of a thousand chariots,
and trust the schemes of slanderers and flatterers,
none have avoided ruin.
Therefore the Book of Songs says:
"Slanderers know no bounds,
they throw the whole land into confusion."
Many villains form cliques,
to deceive the ruler,
the state endangered, the people lost,
is it not fitting?
The Way is greatest in non-action,
conduct is greatest in caution and respect.
Why say so?
In ancient times, Yú Shùn governed the world,
strumming the five-stringed zither,
singing the poems of the "South Wind",
serene as without intent to govern,
indifferent as without concern for the people,
yet the world was greatly ordered.
The Duke of Zhōu created rituals and music,
sacrificed to heaven and earth,
paid homage to mountains and rivers,
without deploying armies,
with punishments set aside and laws suspended,
and within the four seas,
tributes came arriving,
the rulers of Yuècháng,
through interpreters, came to court.
Thus, non-action is indeed action.
Qín Shǐhuáng established penal laws,
instituting the punishment of tearing apart by chariots,
to suppress wickedness and evil.
He built the Great Wall on the borders of the Róng tribes,
to defend against the Hú and Yuè peoples,
conquering the large and swallowing the small,
his might shaking the world.
Generals and commanders roamed unchecked,
subjugating foreign states.
Méng Tián suppressed rebellions abroad,
while Lǐ Sī enforced laws at home.
The more numerous the affairs became,
the more chaotic the world grew.
The more laws proliferated, the more rampant wickedness became;
the more troops and horses were deployed, the more enemies increased.
It was not that Qín did not wish to govern well,
but what it failed in
was due to imposing harsh measures on the masses
and employing punishments too extremely.
Therefore, the noble person values generosity and ease to nurture their character,
cultivating a balanced and harmonious demeanor to attract those distant;
the people fear their authority and follow their transformation,
cherish their virtue and return to their realm,
admire their governance and dare not oppose their rule.
The people fear punishment without being penalized,
and are encouraged without rewards,
gradually immersed in the Way and Virtue,
and clothed in the effects of balance and harmony.
Laws and decrees are meant to punish evil,
not to encourage goodness.
Thus, the filial piety of Zēng and Mǐn,
the integrity of Yí and Qí—
were these done out of fear of death?
They were the result of cultivation and transformation.
Hence it is said:
The people of Yáo and Shùn
could be enfeoffed house by house;
the people of Jié and Zhòu
could be executed house by house.
Why?
Cultivation and transformation made them so.
Thus, the land near rivers is damp,
and the soil near mountains is dry,
because like affects like.
Therefore, mountains and rivers produce clouds and rain,
hills and mounds generate vital energy,
the four great rivers flow east,
and no streams run west—
the small follow the large,
and the few follow the many.
The capital of the true king,
the ruler facing south,
is where the common people look for models and rules.
Their actions and movements
must not lose these models and rules.
In the past,
King Xiāng of Zhōu could not serve his stepmother properly,
and went to reside in Zhèng,
leading those below to often betray their own kin.
Qín Shǐhuáng was arrogant, extravagant, and ostentatious,
fond of building high towers and pavilions,
and expanding palaces and halls.
Then, the wealthy and powerful across the land, in constructing their houses,
all imitated him,
setting up inner chambers,
preparing stables and storehouses,
indulging in the art of carving and engraving,
and vying for dark, yellow, and rare jade colors,
thereby disrupting the proper regulations.
Duke Huán of Qí favored the beauty of women,
marrying his aunts and sisters,
and within the state, many committed incest.
King Píng of Chǔ was extravagant and self-indulgent,
unable to control those below,
or restrain the people with virtue.
He increased his carriage team to a hundred horses when traveling,
wishing to make the people of the world amass wealth and profit,
showing it was unattainable.
Thereupon, Chǔ grew ever more extravagant,
with no distinction between ruler and ministers.
Thus, the transformation from above to below
is like the wind bending the grass.
If the king emphasizes martial prowess at court,
then farmers will repair armor and weapons in the fields.
Therefore, when the noble person governs those below,
if the people are extravagant,
they respond with frugality;
if they are arrogant and dissolute,
they regulate them with principle.
There has never been a case where those above were benevolent and those below were thieving,
or those above were righteous and those below were contentious.
Hence, Confucius said:
"Transform customs and change habits."
How could it be by making each household see it?
It is simply by drawing from oneself.
Those who undertake affairs may do good but not be praised,
or do evil but be praised.
Why?
Because the observers are mistaken and the commentators are in error.
Thus, actions may conform to the world,
words may please the ear,
but this is merely flattering the ruler's intentions,
following the ruler's wishes,
holding to straightness yet deviating from the right path,
harboring crookedness yet aligning with evil,
adapting to the tendencies of strength and weakness,
devising strategies of vertical and horizontal alliances.
Hence, there are no words of opposition,
and no meanings that do not conform.
In the past, Duke Āi asked Yǒu Ruò:
"The harvest is poor,
and resources are insufficient.
What should be done?"
Yǒu Ruò replied:
"Why not reduce the tax to one-tenth?"
This meant reducing the upper to benefit the lower,
which was displeasing to the ear and did not accord with the duke's wishes,
so it was rejected and not adopted.
This is what is called correcting one's actions without heedlessly conforming to the world.
Did Yǒu Ruò not know how to flatter Duke Āi's intentions
for the sake of benefiting the state?
The noble person acts with straightforward principles,
knowing they will face disgrace yet not avoiding it.
Thus, in action, they dare not conform heedlessly;
in speech, they do not seek heedless approval.
Though they may achieve no merit in the world,
their name is worthy of praise;
though their words may not be used by the state,
their actions and words can serve as a model.
Therefore, differing from worldly customs,
they become isolated among the masses.
When the crooked and evil support each other,
and the unjust and twisted interweave,
the upright naturally find no place among them.
When the flattering and sycophantic bolster each other,
and slanderous mouths praise one another,
there is no height they cannot reach,
no depth they cannot penetrate. Why?
Because their factions are numerous,
and their words harmonize in agreement.
The praise and blame of many mouths
can make stones float and wood sink.
A crowd of evil ones suppressing together
can turn straight into crooked.
If one looks without careful examination,
white may be taken for black.
The difference between crooked and straight in form,
the distinction between white and black in color,
are among the easiest things to see in the world,
yet the eyes err and the mind is confused.
If one cannot clearly distinguish right from wrong,
it is because the many evil ones have misled them.
As for the time of Qín Èrshì,
Zhào Gāo drove a deer in his procession.
The king said:
"Why is the chancellor driving a deer?"
Gāo said:
"It is a horse."
The king said:
"The chancellor is mistaken;
you are taking a deer for a horse."
Gāo said:
"It is indeed a horse.
If Your Majesty does not believe my words,
I ask to inquire of the ministers."
Thereupon, he asked the ministers,
and half said it was a deer,
half said it was a horse.
At that moment,
the king of Qín could not trust his own eyes,
and followed the words of the treacherous ministers.
The difference in form between a horse and a deer
is something known to all,
yet he could not distinguish right from wrong.
How much more so for obscure and murky matters?
The *Yìjīng* says:
"When two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut metal."
When a faction unites in purpose
to topple a single ruler,
who would not be swayed?
There was once a man who shared the same name as Zēngzǐ and committed murder.
Someone informed his mother, saying:
"Shēn has killed a man."
His mother continued weaving as before.
After a while,
the person came again to tell her,
and this happened three times.
Then Zēngzǐ's mother threw down her shuttle, climbed over the wall, and fled.
It wasn't that Zēngzǐ's mother didn't know her son wouldn't kill anyone,
but those saying so were numerous.
When slanderous words come repeatedly,
and many people affirm or deny something,
even the wise and virtuous dare not remain self-assured,
let alone ordinary people?
During the time of Duke Dìng of Lǔ,
he met with the Marquis of Qí at Jiāgǔ,
and Kǒngzǐ served as the ceremonial director.
The two rulers ascended the platform,
their ministers stood below,
and the directors exchanged bows.
The rituals between ruler and subject
were fully observed with great dignity.
Then the people of Qí shouted and rose up,
intending to seize the Duke of Lǔ.
Kǒngzǐ ascended the steps,
stopping one step from the top, and declared
to the Marquis of Qí:
"Two rulers meet for friendly relations,
leading each other with ritual,
transforming each other with music.
I have heard that fine music should not be performed in the wild,
and ritual vessels should not descend from the hall.
What do the barbarians seek here?"
He ordered the Minister of War to stop them.
Duke Dìng said:
"So be it."
The Marquis of Qí hesitated, rose from his mat, and said:
"This is my fault."
He withdrew and blamed his own ministers.
The meeting was adjourned.
The people of Qí sent entertainers to dance below the tent of the Duke of Lǔ,
acting arrogantly and playfully,
hoping to find an opening with the ruler of Lǔ
to seize Duke Dìng.
Kǒngzǐ sighed and said:
"When the ruler is insulted,
the minister should die."
He ordered the Minister of War to carry out the law and behead them,
so that their heads and feet exited through different gates.
Thereupon, the people of Qí were struck with fear,
ruler and ministers changed their conduct,
uneasy with their former ways,
and returned the four districts of land they had seized from Lǔ.
They ultimately lost any intention to invade Lǔ,
neighboring states were shaken,
people cherished thoughts of turning to Lǔ,
arrogant rulers of powerful states
all became fearful,
treacherous and flattering ministers
changed their behavior and reconsidered,
and the governance of the world
found its mean through this.
Yet Duke Dìng was constrained by the Three Families,
trapped by public opinion,
and unable to fully employ Kǒngzǐ,
because inwardly he lacked the insight of independent judgment,
and outwardly he was misled by factions of treacherous ministers,
weakening his state and leading to his own demise,
with power falling to the Three Families,
and territory diminished before powerful Qí.
To employ men in such a way,
and lose men in such a manner;
yet Duke Dìng remained unawakened,
trusting in Jìsūn's schemes,
turning his back on the strategies of loyal ministers,
thereby earning a reputation for being constrained and weak,
and losing achievements as weighty as mountains,
is that not deluded indeed!
Thus, the way treacherous ministers obscure the worthy
is like floating clouds blocking the sun and moon.
Unless transformed by divine spirit,
dispersing the clouds and clearing the obscurity,
making them retreat to the mountains and seas,
only then can we see their brightness,
drying the dampness across the world,
and illuminating the gloom in all directions.
Now, above there are no enlightened kings or sage rulers,
below there are no loyal and upright feudal lords
to eradicate the factions of treacherous ministers and rebels,
or untie the knots of doubt and error.
Only then can loyal, good, upright, and honest men
find acceptance in the world and implement governance.
Thus, Kǒngzǐ encountered a dim-witted ruler and chaotic ministers,
with many evil ones in positions of power,
the way of governance blocked by the Three Families,
and benevolence and righteousness shut out from the court.
Therefore, he composed the song "Gōnglíng",
grieving that he had no power in the world,
the great transformation severed and blocked,
and the way of virtue promoted but not applied.
Hence it is said:
"When there is nothing to be done,
I too can do nothing about it."
For the Way stands by authority,
and virtue moves through influence.
Those not in position
cannot regulate governance,
and those not holding the handle
cannot control its strength.
The Book of Songs says:
"Have the axe, have the handle."
This speaks of how to govern.
Those who achieve great merits in the world must first cultivate within their own households,
and those who leave a great name for ten thousand generations must first act in the smallest matters.
Thus, Yī Yǐn carried his cauldron,
humbling himself in the wilds of Yǒushēn,
cultivating far-reaching virtue beneath a thatched hut,
personally engaging in farmers' work,
while harboring the way of emperors in his heart,
his body within a humble gate,
yet his ambition reaching to the eight extremes.
Therefore, he set aside his intention of carrying the cauldron
to become the assistant to the Son of Heaven,
overthrew Xià and established Shāng,
punished the rebellious and campaigned against the violent,
eliminated the troubles of the world,
and expelled the cruel and harmful kinds.
Only then did the land within the seas become orderly, and the common people peaceful.
Zēngzǐ was filial to his parents,
ensuring their comfort at night and greeting them in the morning,
adjusting to the cold and warm,
balancing the light and heavy,
persevering in the details of congee and porridge,
and practicing it on the mat and bedding.
Thus, his virtuous beauty became revered by later generations.
These two examples
were cultivated internally
and manifested externally;
practiced in small matters
and revealed in great ones.
Yán Huí, with a single basket of food,
a single gourd of drink,
living in a humble alley,
where others could not have endured the hardship,
Yán Huí never changed his joy.
Act with ritual,
express with humility.
Now, studying diligently and reciting the "Shī" and "Shū",
is something anyone can do;
but if one wishes to move rivers and lakes,
shift Mount Tài,
that is indeed beyond human capability.
If one regulates the mind within oneself,
turns from evil towards good,
does not covet wealth,
does not seek improper gain,
takes less in dividing resources,
undertakes labor in service,
these are principles easily understood by all under heaven,
easily practiced deeds,
how could they be difficult?
Like Zàofǔ's skill in driving horses,
or Yì's mastery of the crossbow,
that is what is called difficult.
The noble person does not engage in what is difficult for its own sake,
thus not knowing it is considered good,
renouncing physical strength,
and esteeming virtue.
If the eyes cannot distinguish black from white,
the ears cannot discern clear from muddy sounds,
the mouth cannot speak of good and evil,
that is what is called incapability.
Therefore, those who establish the Way make it easily understood,
so as to connect with the hearts of ordinary people,
and achieve what the incapable cannot perform.
The Way is what humans practice.
The great Way is trodden and followed,
then nothing is impossible,
hence it is called the Way.
Confucius said:
"The Way is not practiced."
Meaning people cannot follow it.
Thus he said to Yán Yuān:
"When employed, practice it;
when cast aside, conceal it;
only you and I have this ability."
Meaning Yán Yuān's Way was applicable to the world but none used it.
Like those who cannot embrace benevolence and practice righteousness,
distinguish subtleties,
contemplate heaven and earth,
instead torment their bodies and labor their forms,
enter deep mountains,
seek immortals,
abandon their parents,
forsake kin,
abstain from the five grains,
discard the "Shī" and "Shū",
reject the treasures of heaven and earth,
pursue the path to immortality,
this is not the way to navigate the world and prevent wrongdoing.
Like the rulers Tāng and Wǔ,
ministers Yī and Lǚ,
who administered punishments according to heavenly timing,
acted in harmony with yīn and yáng,
observed celestial patterns above,
examined human hearts below,
subdued the many with few,
controlled the strong with weakness,
with three hundred war chariots,
three thousand armored soldiers,
conquered enemies and defeated multitudes,
avenged great grievances,
punished rebellious and chaotic rulers,
eradicated the source of turmoil and corruption,
brought peace and harmony to the world,
ensured households were provided for and people satisfied,
commoners practiced benevolence,
merchants acted with integrity,
aligned with heaven and earth,
commanded spirits and gods,
the River produced the diagram,
the Luò yielded the writing,
through this Way,
entrusted between heaven and earth,
is this not what ancient times called attaining the Way?
Those who spread coarse cloth,
tangle their hair,
climb high mountains,
eat tree fruits,
appear without graceful demeanor,
speak without benevolent or righteous words,
absent-minded like mad or foolish,
unmoved when pushed,
unresponsive when pulled,
contributing nothing to their time,
leaving no talent for posterity,
not supporting toppling rulers,
not upholding endangered states,
lonely without neighbors,
vast and solitary in sleep,
may be called world-avoiders,
not those who embrace the Way.
Thus, sacrificing oneself to avoid hardship is unwise,
and embracing the Way to shun the world is disloyal.
Therefore, the noble person in chaotic times
unites with the moral way,
adopts minor virtues,
eliminates subtle evils,
cultivates the ritual between father and son,
and extends to the order between ruler and minister,
which is the universal path of heaven and earth,
never abandoned by sages.
Thus concealed, it is the Way;
spread, it becomes culture;
in the heart as poetry, it is will;
spoken aloud, it becomes words;
corrected with elegance,
sharpening dull talents,
carving literary brilliance,
resolving doubts,
smoothing obstacles and理顺 principles,
distinguishing right from wrong,
so that emotions are harmonized,
and nature is governed,
continuously and imperceptibly,
restrained by the Way,
inspected without signs,
vanishing vast and seamless,
its actions unseen,
its benevolence unobserved,
profoundly unawakened,
only differentiated over time,
contemplating heaven and earth,
moving in response to pivotal mechanisms,
bowing and rising, advancing and retreating,
in harmony with the Way,
stored within oneself,
leisurely awaiting the time.
Thus, the Way is never abandoned without revival,
and vessels never destroyed without restoration.
Confucius said:
"There is the highest virtue and essential Way to harmonize the world."
Meaning when virtue is practiced, those below will comply.
Those of fine substance value being known;
those of excellent talent take prominence as ability.
Why is this said?
Take piánnán and yùzhāng, famous woods of the world,
born deep within mountains,
produced beside streams and valleys.
Standing, they become the ancestors of Tàishān's multitude of trees;
felled, they serve for ten thousand generations.
Floating upon mountain streams,
emerging from obscure wilderness,
following the courses of the Jiāng and Hé rivers,
they reach beneath the capital city.
Through the work of axes,
they display their beautiful patterns.
Strong and straight-grained,
dense and versatile,
insects and scorpions cannot bore through them,
water and damp cannot harm them.
When high up, they are pliant;
when in the ground, they are firm.
Without oil or polish, they gleam with luster;
without carving or painting, patterns form.
Above, they become imperial possessions;
below, they are bestowed upon high ministers.
Commoners and lowly people may not use them for tools.
But if blocked by passes and bridges,
hindered by the obstacles of mountain slopes,
separated by the embankments of Jiǔzōng,
fallen upon towering peaks,
stranded in deep, dark streams,
where trees grow thick and tangled without gaps,
and rocks stand jagged and unyielding,
broad areas lack access by boat or cart,
narrow paths lack even footpaths,
where merchants do not go,
craftsmen do not look,
the knowledgeable do not see,
and those who see do not know,
their merit is abandoned, their virtue lost,
rotting and withering,
tumbling into hundred-ren chasms,
lying alone in fear,
at such a time,
they are not even as good as a withered poplar by the roadside.
Crooked and winding,
bent and uneven,
yet if born in the broad lands of a great capital,
close to the famous craftsmen of great artisans,
then their material is shaped and cut,
measured by compass and square,
the hard used to mend the rotten,
the short extended to length,
the large made into zūn vessels,
the small into shāng cups,
adorned with red lacquer,
polished to brightness,
above, prepared for the Tàiláo sacrifice,
in spring and autumn ceremonies at the school,
praised for their patterns,
standing in solemn dignity for rites,
capped and belted,端正 in appearance,
facing wine, passing cups,
with ministers and officials arrayed in ranks,
displayed in the palace hall,
those who look are dazzled,
those near smell their fragrance.
Thus, if affairs are blocked, they are cut off;
if promoted, they thrive.
Suppressed, they sink;
raised, they soar.
Pián and zǐ trees in their place
are inferior to withered poplars.
It is not that their virtue and beauty are not vastly different,
nor that their talent and strength are not far apart.
One is dried and cast away,
while the other becomes the húliǎn vessels of the ancestral temple—
all due to being known or unknown.
So it is with people too.
Consider the people of remote marshes,
those who grasp plows and handle plowshares.
Some may harbor untamable talent,
possessing the virtues of Yáo, Shùn, and Gāo Yáo,
with principles upheld in their persons,
and techniques for ten thousand generations hidden in their hearts.
Yet they are not employed by the world,
because there is no one to introduce and make them known.
As for the sons of high ministers,
the friends and partisans of nobles,
though they may lack exceptional talent,
yet being in respected positions,
with strong supporters and skillful embellishers,
none fail to achieve prominence.
In the past, Biǎn Què lived in Sòng,
offended the lord of Sòng,
and fled to Wèi.
A man in Wèi was ill and near death;
Biǎn Què went to his home,
wishing to treat him.
The sick man's father said to Biǎn Què:
"My son is gravely ill;
I am about to fetch a good doctor to treat him—
it is not something you can cure."
He sent him away unused,
and instead had a spirit-medium pray for blessings and life,
chanting against Biǎn Què.
The sick man died in the end,
for the spirit-medium could not cure him.
Now Biǎn Què was a fine doctor of the world,
yet he could not compete with the spirit-medium for employment—
all due to being recognized or not.
Thus, seeking the distant and losing the near,
broadly storing yet narrowly discarding,
this is what it means.
In the past, Gōng Zhī Qí advised the Duke of Yú,
urging him to decline the bribe of jade and horses from Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
and not to lend him the Xià Yáng road.
Was this not a plan as firm as metal or stone?
Yet the Duke of Yú did not listen,
deluded by the treasure of rare curios.
As for Bào Qiū's moral conduct,
was it not higher than that of Lǐ Sī and Zhào Gāo?
Yet he lived in obscurity under a thatched hut,
and was not recorded by the world,
harmed by glib-tongued ministers.
All people know that good is good,
and evil is evil;
all know that learning benefits oneself,
and that idleness and play do not help in affairs.
Yet those who do otherwise are driven by overflowing desires,
and cannot overcome their will.
No ruler fails to know he should seek worthies to aid himself,
and draw near to worthies for support;
yet sages and worthies may hide in fields and villages,
not participating in state affairs,
because the ministers who observe and report do not clarify matters below,
and thus the blame for闭塞 falls on the ruler;
when the blame for闭塞 falls on the ruler,
then loyal and worthy scholars are abandoned in the wilds;
when loyal and worthy scholars are abandoned in the wilds,
then the faction of sycophantic ministers remains at court;
when the faction of sycophantic ministers remains at court,
then those below are not loyal to the ruler;
when those below are not loyal to the ruler,
then those above do not understand those below;
when those above do not understand those below,
this is why the world topples.
To enrich the state and strengthen its might,
expand territory and subdue distant lands,
one must gain it from the people;
to achieve merit and raise renown,
leave a lasting name, shed flowing light, and display glory,
one must take it from oneself.
Thus, to rule a state of ten thousand chariots,
hold the lives of the hundred surnames,
possess the abundance of mountains and marshes,
master the strength of the masses,
yet have no merit to oneself,
and no fame prominent in the world—
this is due to errors in governance.
By the nature of heaven and earth,
among the myriad kinds of things,
those who uphold the Way are followed by the masses;
those who rely on punishment are feared by the people.
Those followed draw others close;
those feared make people leave their domain.
Therefore, in establishing punishments, one cannot be too light;
in practicing virtue, one cannot be too weighty;
in administering penalties, one need not worry about being meager;
in distributing rewards, one need not worry about being generous—
this is how to draw the near and attract the distant.
When punishments are severe, the mind becomes troubled;
when affairs are numerous, the body becomes weary.
A troubled mind leads to punishments being applied arbitrarily without proper foundation,
a weary body results in all manner of deviousness without achievement.
Therefore, when the gentleman governs,
he appears solid as if without affairs,
silent as if without sound,
the government offices as if without officials,
the villages as if without people.
In the neighborhoods, there are no disputes in the lanes;
the old and young do not grieve in the courtyards.
Those nearby have nothing to debate,
those far away have nothing to hear.
The postal stations have no officials traveling at night,
the rural communities have no emergency conscriptions.
Dogs do not bark at night,
chickens do not crow at night.
The elderly enjoy fine flavors in their halls,
the able-bodied plow and weed in the fields.
Those in court are loyal to their ruler,
those at home are filial to their parents.
Then good is rewarded and evil punished, enhancing this order,
schools are established to educate and instruct,
after which the wise and foolish have different views,
the honest and base are classified differently,
elders and youth have distinct etiquette,
superiors and inferiors have differentiation,
the strong and weak support each other,
the small and large cherish each other,
the noble and humble succeed one another,
following like wild geese in flight.
Though he does not speak, he is trusted;
though he does not anger, he is awe-inspiring.
How could this depend on strong armor and sharp weapons, harsh punishments and severe laws, urgent measures day and night to be achieved?
In the past, Jìn Lì, Qí Zhuāng, Chǔ Líng, and Sòng Xiāng,
holding the authority of great states,
wielding the power of numerous people,
sent out armies arbitrarily,
trampled on the feudal lords,
were arrogant toward enemy states abroad,
oppressive to the common people at home.
Abroad, they incurred the enmity of neighboring states,
at home, they accumulated the resentment of their ministers.
Yet they wished to establish achievements as enduring as metal and stone,
to pass on an unending lineage,
was this not difficult indeed?
Thus Sòng Xiāng died at the battle of Hóngshuǐ,
the other three rulers were assassinated by their ministers or sons.
All lightly employed military force and valued power,
leading to such outcomes.
Therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals emphasized and recorded this,
sighing and lamenting over it.
These three rulers all strengthened their might but lost their states,
intensified their punishments but brought ruin upon themselves.
This serves as a warning from past events and a lesson for future ones.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ within a single year,
during three seasons initiated construction projects,
planned profits from forests and marshes,
competed with the people for the bounty of fields, fishing, and firewood gathering.
He carved rafters and painted pillars red,
creating dazzling extravagance,
collected a twelve-percent tax from the people,
yet it was insufficient to satisfy his devious desires.
He maintained unnecessary luxuries,
to please women's eyes,
wealth was exhausted on arrogance and excess,
human effort was wasted on non-urgent matters.
The ruler was strained for resources,
the people starved for food.
Then he sent Zāngsūn Chén to request emergency supplies from Qí,
granaries were empty and depleted,
outsiders learned of this,
whereupon he was attacked by Qí, Wèi, Chén, and Sòng.
Worthy ministers departed,
treacherous ministers caused chaos,
Zǐ Bān was killed,
and the state of Lǔ was endangered.
Gōngzǐ Yá, Qìngfǔ and their followers,
destroyed the order between superior and inferior,
confused the distinction between men and women,
leaving no certainty about succession,
and no fear among rebels and troublemakers.
Then Duke Huán of Qí sent his minister Gāo Zǐ to establish Duke Xī and execute the lady,
expelled Qìngfǔ and restored Jì Zǐ,
after which the altars of soil and grain were preserved,
descendants returned to their proper occupations.
Can this not be said to show what happens when a state is weak?
Thus, asserting authority without strength leads to self-destruction,
establishing laws without clarity leads to self-harm,
as exemplified by Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ.
Therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals criticize this.
Those with divided thoughts cannot establish plans,
those holding two positions cannot determine authority.
Thus, to govern external affairs one must harmonize internal ones,
to pacify distant regions one must rectify nearby ones.
To regulate the world,
laboring one's spirit across the eight extremes,
means worries do not remain within the household.
To cultivate vital energy and govern one's nature,
thinking to penetrate the essence-spirit,
to extend lifespan,
means the will is not enslaved by external matters.
Occupying territory and governing the people,
ruling the state and managing the masses,
one should not scheme for profit,
or manage private estates,
otherwise education and transformation will not be implemented,
and governmental decrees will not be followed.
Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí,
though personally esteemed in position,
and renowned in their time,
served as ministers to six states,
attended six rulers,
their prestige shook the area east of the mountains,
they persuasively debated with the feudal lords,
with different words for each state,
different ideas for each person,
wanting to unite the weak to control the strong,
to maintain horizontal alliances to counter vertical ones,
yet internally they had no firm strategy,
personally they had no settled reputation,
their achievements were unstable,
they were abandoned midway,
died at the hands of ordinary men,
and were laughed at by the world,
precisely because their words were inconsistent,
and their passions were unrestrained.
Thus Guǎn Zhòng served Duke Huán,
humbling himself to serve his ruler,
concentrating with single-minded devotion,
having no external connections personally,
no crooked thoughts in his heart.
He rectified his state as if regulating the world,
honored his ruler and subdued the feudal lords,
his influence operated throughout the realm,
his transformation flowed to all Chinese states,
those who lost the Way were punished,
those who upheld righteousness were elevated,
when he initiated one undertaking the world followed,
when he issued one policy the feudal lords complied.
Therefore the sage holds to one policy to regulate the common people,
maintains one standard to equalize the myriad people,
thereby unifying governance and clarifying unity.
Thus heaven's unity completes numbers,
humanity's unity completes order.
King Líng of Chǔ inhabited a thousand-mile territory,
enjoyed a state of a hundred cities,
yet did not prioritize humaneness and righteousness or honor the Way and virtue,
instead cherished unusual skills,
... yīn-yáng,
combined with strange phenomena,
built the Gānxī Tower,
erected it hundreds of ren high,
wanting to climb the floating clouds,
observe the patterns of heaven,
yet he died at the hands of Qìjí.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ occupied central territory,
succeeded the legacy of sages,
yet did not cultivate the work of Zhōu Gōng,
continue the system of his predecessors,
instead valued authority and relied on power,
possessed the strength of ten thousand men,
harbored ambition to surpass others,
yet could not preserve or establish Zǐ Jiū,
the state was invaded, territory seized,
reduced to the boundaries of the Zhū and Sì rivers.
Nowadays people do not study the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
practice humaneness and righteousness,
honor the Way of the sages,
exhaust the depths of classical arts,
instead discuss unverifiable words,
study impractical matters,
chart the forms of heaven and earth,
explain disasters and anomalies,
deviate from the laws of former kings,
differ from the intentions of sages,
confuse the minds of learners,
shift the aspirations of the masses,
point to heaven and sketch the earth,
judge right and wrong in worldly affairs,
move people with evil changes,
startle people with strange wonders,
listeners regard it as divine,
viewers see it as extraordinary;
yet still it cannot help them through difficulties or save themselves,
some violate the law ...
and cannot avoid punishment and execution.
Therefore, affairs not born from laws and measures,
ways not rooted in heaven and earth,
may be spoken of but not practiced,
may be listened to but not transmitted,
may be ... but not greatly used.
Thus, what is permissible for things
is not what is appropriate for the Way;
what is appropriate for the Way,
is not what is permissible for things.
Therefore, those who manage affairs cannot be wavering,
those who establish the Way cannot be inconsistent.
The eyes are for clarity and brightness,
the ears for controlling hearing,
the mouth for distinguishing flavors,
the nose for detecting fragrances,
the hands for holding,
the feet for walking,
each endowed with a single nature,
unable to combine two functions;
combining two leads to confusion of the heart,
pursuing two paths leads to a dead end,
with a steadfast and focused heart,
long-lasting and unforgettable,
those above do not become idle,
those below do not suffer harm,
grasping unity to govern all things,
even if few, they will become many;
if the heart is idle and emotions scattered,
even if high, they will collapse,
vital energy leaks away, giving rise to illness,
lifespan will not be long,
topsy-turvy without order,
losing the Way, progress halts.
Thus, the sign of vital energy's influence,
is pure, clean, bright, and luminous,
the expression of genuine emotions,
is calm, smooth, harmonious, and good,
those well-regulated and meticulous are stable,
those tranquil and quiet are auspicious,
will settled and heart peaceful,
then the blood vessels become strong,
in governing, aiming for duality,
loses its central standard,
warriors do not farm,
court officials do not trade,
the crooked does not interfere with the straight,
the round does not disrupt the square,
contradictions and conflicts intermingle,
disorder and discord are hard to rectify.
Hence, a ruler who desires order
closes the gate to profit,
a family that accumulates virtue
will surely have no disaster or calamity,
profit ceases and the Way becomes evident,
military yields and virtue flourishes,
this is the way to endure long,
the constant practice of the method.
Governance takes the Dào and virtue as supreme,
conduct takes benevolence and righteousness as foundation.
Thus, those honored in position but without virtue are dismissed,
those rich in wealth but without righteousness are punished,
the lowly who love virtue are honored,
the poor who possess righteousness are esteemed.
Duàngān Mù, a scholar on foot,
cultivated the Dào and practiced virtue,
Wèi Wén Hóu passed by his lane and bowed to his crossbar.
When the Master was in distress between Chén and Cài,
eating bean meals and vegetable soup,
insufficient to stave off hunger,
his disciples in worn-out hemp robes and padded garments,
unable to ward off the cold,
harassed and in dire straits,
they endured extreme hardship;
yet the Master held fast to the Dào,
and his disciples adhered to righteousness,
from scholars in common cloth clothes,
up to the Son of Heaven,
down to the ordinary people,
they burdened themselves to rectify those above.
Concerned about the decline of the Zhōu court,
and the neglect of ritual and righteousness,
suffering setbacks and stumbling,
he traveled persuading various lords,
seeking to rectify the way of emperors and kings,
reverse the governance under heaven,
with no position for himself,
and no sovereign in the world recognizing him,
he roamed throughout the realm,
finding no one who shared his ideals,
the great Dào hidden and not extended,
wings broken and not stretched out,
he deeply imparted its transformations to order the beginning and end,
traced past events to correct the future,
examined records and charts to understand nature and destiny,
established the "Six Arts" to emphasize Confucian teachings,
so that good and evil do not interfere,
noble and humble do not insult each other,
strong and weak do not oppress one another,
the worthy and unworthy cannot surpass their places,
ranked in proper order,
continuing unbroken for ten thousand generations,
achievements passed down without decline,
the "Book of Songs," "Book of Documents," "Rites," and "Music,"
each in its proper place,
are what Heaven's Dào establishes,
and great righteousness practices.
How could it be due to authority and power?
A person's beauty
cannot be adorned by cosmetics;
the awe of great anger
cannot be exerted by mere force.
The sage rides Heaven's awe,
harmonizes with Heaven's energy,
undertakes Heaven's tasks,
emulates Heaven's countenance,
yet does not claim credit for the achievements,
is that not difficult?
Having a pool of wine to boat on,
a hill of dregs to gaze afar from,
how could that be poverty in wealth?
Holding the power over all within the seas,
ruling the masses of the nine provinces,
how could that be weakness in military force?
Yet, achievements cannot preserve themselves, and power cannot maintain itself,
not because of poverty or weakness,
but because Dào and virtue are not upheld personally,
and benevolence and righteousness are not extended to the world.
Thus, those clear about wealth but blind to the Dào
are targeted by the masses;
those resolute in force but lacking in righteousness
are plotted against by soldiers.
Hence, the gentleman is devoted to righteousness and indifferent to profit,
diligent in actions and cautious in words,
thereby broadening merit and virtue.
Therefore it is said:
"Wealth and honor attained through unrighteousness
are to me as floating clouds."
Wearing jade pendants on the body,
girded with circular ornaments,
clad in famous treasures,
hiding rare curiosities,
using jade vessels to pour wine,
golden goblets intricately carved,
may dazzle the eyes of petty people,
but do not truly benefit oneself or aid in affairs.
High terraces of a hundred ren,
gilded walls with painted patterns,
curtains exquisitely carved and adorned,
serve to exhaust the people's strength,
not to support the weak or preserve the perishing.
Thus, the sage humbles his palace but elevates Dào and virtue,
disdains fine clothes but upholds benevolence and righteousness,
does not impair his conduct to enhance his appearance,
does not compromise his virtue to adorn his person,
the state does not undertake useless projects,
the family does not hoard useless objects,
thereby reducing labor and minimizing tributes.
If jade and pearls are not used by the ruler,
then objects of frivolous pleasure are abandoned by the subjects;
if carvings and engravings are not accepted by the lord,
then excessive craftsmanship and cunning skills cease among the people.
Abandoning farming and sericulture,
venturing into mountains and seas,
gathering pearls and gems,
seeking precious stones,
exploring sandy valleys,
catching kingfishers,
hunting for hawksbill turtles,
capturing rhinoceroses and elephants,
consuming sinew and strength,
scattering coins,
to satisfy the pleasures of eyes and ears,
to gratify wanton and corrupt hearts,
is that not absurd?
Never has one been seen who prioritizes the Dào and neglects profit,
who draws near to virtue and keeps away from sensuality.
If the ruler is enlightened in governance,
he can influence far and wide;
if the minister is steadfast in trustworthiness,
he can achieve greatness.
Why is this said?
In the past, Tāng with a fief of seventy li
ascended to the position of emperor and king;
the Duke of Zhōu, from the office of the Three Dukes,
matched the virtue of the Five Emperors and Three Kings;
this was the result of speaking good words
and practicing the good Dào personally.
Thus, the effects of safety and danger,
the signs of fortune and misfortune,
all stem from one's person;
the way of survival and perish,
the evidence of success and failure,
all begin with good conduct;
Yáo and Shùn did not change the sun and moon, yet they flourished,
Jié and Zhòu did not change the stars, yet they perished,
Heaven's Dào does not change, but human ways do.
He who holds the governance of heaven and earth,
and grasps the guiding principles of the four seas,
must not lose proper measure in bending or stretching,
nor deviate from the Way in actions.
If erroneous words escape his lips,
chaos will extend ten thousand miles beyond;
how much more so when punishments reach the innocent in prisons,
and executions befall the guiltless in the markets?
Thus, the decline of the age and the loss of the Way
are not acts of Heaven,
but rather what the rulers of states have brought upon themselves.
Evil governance arises from malign influences,
and malign influences stem from calamities and anomalies.
Creatures like venomous snakes
emerge following these influences;
phenomena such as rainbows
appear due to governance.
When the Way of governance is lost below,
heavenly patterns change above;
when evil governance affects the people,
insect plagues arise on earth.
Wise rulers, being intelligent, know to reform according to changes,
contemplate by drawing analogies,
and adapt to transformations.
In the governance of sages,
kindness extends to insects,
and beneficence reaches plants and trees.
All that thrives by the qi of heaven
and moves with the cold and heat
cranes their necks hoping for order,
and pricks up their ears listening for transformation.
Sages observe things
without missing anything,
from the sun, moon, and stars above
to birds, beasts, plants, trees, and insects below.
They note the retreating flight of the yi bird,
and record where the five stones fell,
thus not neglecting the slightest detail.
When the què yù birds come,
or deer abound in winter,
it speaks of anomalies among birds and beasts.
"Peaches and plums fruit in the twelfth month,
frost in the tenth month does not kill beans,"
indicates that the qi of cold and heat
has lost its proper rhythm.
If birds, beasts, plants, and trees all desire their rightful places,
regulated by laws
and ordered by principles,
how much more should humans?
Sages follow Heaven's brilliance,
rectify the courses of the sun and moon,
record the movements of stars,
utilize the benefits of heaven and earth,
assess the suitability of high and low lands,
establish conveniences of mountains and rivers,
pacify the four seas,
divide the nine provinces,
unify likes and dislikes,
and harmonize customs.
The Yì Jīng says:
"Heaven displays images,
revealing good and ill fortune,
and sages emulate them;
Heaven produces the good Way,
and sages obtain it."
This means mastering the changes in prognostic charts and calendars,
and addressing the decline in moral transformation below,
to rectify prosperity and decay,
order things and stabilize the world,
so that thereafter, no governance is unworkable,
and no people are ungovernable.
Hence it is said:
"Emulate Heaven's brilliance,
utilize Earth's benefits."
Observing Heaven's transformations,
inferring the categories of all events,
dispersing them throughout the vastness,
harmonizing them with the rhythms of cold and heat,
nourishing them with the qi of the four seasons,
and uniting them with the influence of wind and rain,
thus even distant lands with different customs
all know to...
sing when joyful,
weep when sorrowful,
for the sage's teachings unify them.
When good conduct resides in a person,
no distance is too far to reach;
when evil deeds mark one's self,
no proximity keeps others from departing.
The Duke of Zhōu personally practiced ritual and righteousness,
sacrificed to Hòu Jì in the suburbs,
and Yuè Cháng brought tribute through multiple translations to arrive,
while qílín, phoenixes, white pheasants, plants, and trees responded through transformation.
When King Zhòu of Yīn was without the Way,
Wēizǐ abandoned his own flesh and blood to flee.
Those who do good please even birds and beasts,
while those who do evil frighten their ministers and sons.
Thus, the enlightened can reach far,
while the base may lose what is near.
Therefore, the Chūn Qiū records that brother Zhuān of the Wèi侯 fled to Jìn,
writing that Zhuān severed kinship ties,
abandoned his position as a senior official,
crossed his ancestors' borders,
attached himself to another's domain,
endured extreme cold and hunger,
and wove sandals to eat—
this is the effect of lack of enlightenment.
Those adept at handling change
cannot be exhausted by deceit.
Those versed in the Way
cannot be startled by the bizarre.
Those discerning with words
cannot be confused by rhetoric.
Those profound in righteousness
cannot be swayed by profit.
Thus, the noble-minded broaden their thoughts and listen extensively,
advance and retreat according to law,
act with proper measure,
hearing and seeing much but selecting carefully,
learning broadly but conducting themselves earnestly,
recognizing the upright by seeing the crooked,
knowing the fruit by observing the flower,
eyes not dazzled by glittering colors,
ears not disturbed by flattering words,
unswayed even by the wealth of Jìn or Chǔ,
unchanged in conduct even when told of the longevity of Wáng Qiáo or Chì Sōng,
thus able to unify their Way and solidify their integrity,
accomplishing their tasks and achieving their merits.
Ordinary people, however,
let their eyes roam over the glory of wealth and honor,
and their ears be confused by paths to immortality,
thus often abandoning their strengths to seek their weaknesses,
failing to gain what they lack while losing what they have.
Therefore, King Fūchāi of Wú knew how to plan victory at Ài Líng,
but did not realize that Zuì Lǐ could lead to his downfall.
Thus, sometimes seeing one advantage leads to losing myriad opportunities,
seeking one blessing brings about myriad misfortunes.
Learners who comprehend the spiritual transformations,
understand the opening and closing of heaven and earth,
the relaxation and tension,
the shortness and length of life,
where wealth and honor lie,
and where poverty and lowliness are lost,
will find their hands and feet untired, ears and eyes unconfused,
thoughts unerring,
strategies unfailing,
deciding right and wrong by heavenly patterns above,
resolving doubts through worldly affairs next,
with foundations for decline and rise,
and principles for change and adaptation,
so the Way... and affairs can be emulated.
In ancient times, Shùn and Yǔ governed the world by building upon prosperity,
while Confucius achieved merit by addressing decline.
Sages do not emerge without cause,
nor are worthies born in vain.
◇◇◇◇◇◇ and all return to goodness,
for this is the way of heaven and earth, which regulates affairs,
adapting to the world's convenience and establishing its principles.
Thus, sages need not follow the same path,
beautiful things need not share the same appearance to be lovely,
nor must ugly things have identical forms to be repulsive.
The patterns of heaven and earth
are manifestations of this mandate.
The sun ◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇ and the twenty-eight constellations align,
each with its own dominion,
myriad paths diverge,
and a thousand methods take different shapes.
Sages harmonize them according to their inherent tendencies,
ensuring that small and large do not overstep,
square and round do not interfere,
dividing them by measure,
ordering them by rhythm,
so stars do not appear by day,
nor the sun shine at night,
thunder does not strike in winter,
frost does not fall in summer.
If ministers do not encroach upon the ruler,
then yin does not invade yang,
midsummer would not be hot,
deep winter would not frost,
dark vapors would not shroud the sun,
comets would not blaze,
rainbows would not appear in winter,
hibernating insects would not hide in summer,
Mars would not disrupt the constellations,
nor would stars stray from their courses.
Sages correct such errors by responding to celestial changes,
straightening the roots by ordering the branches.
Yáo and Shùn, inheriting the failures of Chīyóu,
contemplated the path of reverence and enlightenment.
When the noble person sees evil externally,
they know to transform internally.
If Jié and Zhòu had not been tyrannical,
then Tāng and Wǔ would not have been benevolent.
One corrects faults by discerning the confusion among the masses,
and ◇◇◇◇◇◇◇ chaos in the court,
while commoners manage it within their households.
Thus, Jiēyú and Lǎolái withdrew from the world to remote ◇◇◇◇◇, distancing themselves from honor.
The noble person acts in seclusion,
while the petty person struts before the crowd.
The "Lǎozǐ" says:
"The highest virtue is not conscious of virtue."
◇◇◇◇◇◇ emptiness.
Those who recite the words of sages with their mouths
and practice the actions of worthies with their bodies,
enduring without corruption over time,
laboring without weariness,
though not yet rulers ◇◇◇◇◇◇ enough.
Confucius said:
"Follow the calendar of Xià,
ride in the carriage of Yīn,
wear the ceremonial cap of Zhōu,
and let the music be the Sháo dance.
Banish the tunes of Zhèng,
and keep glib talkers at a distance."
◇◇◇ the Way and practice it in the world,
even if not rulers like Yáo and Shùn,
they become as Yáo and Shùn.
Today's rulers are not so;
they govern not by the methods of the Five Emperors,
claiming the present age cannot be ruled by morality.
Ministers do not emulate the governance of Jì, Qì, and Zhōu Gōng,
saying the people cannot be guided by benevolence and righteousness.
Sons do not uphold the worth of Zēng and Mǐn,
toiling ceaselessly day and night,
exhausting their duty untiringly,
blaming their families for lack of diligence.
Scholars do not grasp the essence of Yán and Cì,
striving unrelentingly day and night,
acting in accordance with ritual,
claiming it is not practiced in the world.
From rulers to commoners,
none fail to emulate sages and learn from worthies,
yet few do good,
while many do evil.
The "Yì Jīng" says:
"He enlarges his house,
covers his home,
peers through the door,
and it is still, with no one there."
'No one' does not mean absence of people,
but that there are no sages or worthies to govern.
Thus, with benevolent persons in power, benevolent people come;
with righteous persons at court, righteous scholars arrive.
Hence, Mòzǐ's school had many brave warriors,
Confucius's disciples excelled in morality,
the courts of Wén and Wǔ abounded in worthies,
while the Qín king's court was full of ominous signs.
Therefore, good must have a focus to arrive,
and evil must have a cause to come.
Good and evil do not emerge without reason,
nor do fortune and misfortune occur randomly,
but solely follow the heart's direction and the will's pursuit.
